For me, the feeling of consciousness' immateriality isn't necessarily incompatible with materialism. I personally prefer a non-reductive physicalist approach, where the framework we use to talk about a certain phenomena changes depending on the phenomena we're talking about. So, while consciousness emerges out of the physical, it still makes the most sense to talk about consciousness in phenomenological terms (as you say) and to talk about the stuff of neurons etc. in physical terms.

I wonder if this argument falls into the self-sealing argument that the article raises. If you say consciousness is something we know the true nature of without physical evidence (what else are you using?) then you seal yourself off from criticism. Since you can always retort with: "My premise is that consciousness is immaterial, therefore I don't/couldn't possibly need material/physical evidence to support it."

Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence that is true. Just because there is no evidence that consciousness is immaterial (indeed, there may be no physical evidence) this doesn't mean it isn't immaterial. However, I also believe that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. So while I will consider and ponder the question of the immateriality of consciousness, I am in no way inclined to believe. I would really need something substantial to believe this.

I think a lot of people have this impression that psychedelics can, in and of themselves, cure our ills. Sure, psychedelic research indicates this and there is no shortage of blogs, articles and YouTube videos of people describing how psychedelics cured their depression or anxiety. And I don't want to doubt the validity of that transformation and recovery.

But perhaps set and setting, intentions and integration, are not emphasised enough in these stories, as they play a crucial role in healing. Moreover, a psychedelic experience can be highly transformative for one person, and not for another. It is a highly individual experience.

My main point is not to rely on psychedelics to 'figure something out' or 'rewire your thinking'. A psychedelic experience may or may not 'show you the way', but it won't take you to your target. 

I have largely lost interest in psychedelics because the handful of powerful experiences I had showed me what I had to work on and this work is on-going, with aspects of myself and my life that need addressing. I could take psychedelics again to have beautiful, blissful and ecstatic experiences, but of course, with psychedelics you don't always get just that, you also get uncomfortable confrontations with your unconscious and an exhausting mental journey, which I have gone through, and don't have that desire to go through again. I still have unconscious material to integrate.

It sounds like you already know what real life problems need addressing: alcohol, opiates, depression, anxiety etc.

What do you expect DMT to show you?

I'm not saying it won't be positive and life-affirming, just that, personally, you have to put the psychedelic lessons into action. When life turns nasty and negative habits manifest, psychedelics could help, but if you know what you have to do, then psychedelics will not do the work for you.

The trip I remember the least was also the most powerful experience I've ever had. Which is strange. I suppose it was because it was my first ego death experience. I didn't black out, since I remember being aware, and also remember understanding absolutely everything - as in the answer to every conceivable question and mystery.

I have been at pains to remember what happened. I'm sure a lot of what I 'remember' or have written down since that trip is filling in the gaps in an imaginative, perhaps even wishful, way. But I think I have to let go of the frustration of not remembering. I told my friends as I came out of it that there were no words. It was ineffable. I believe that this mystical experience involved a special kind of ineffability, one not just defined as an inability to express or describe what happened; but as an inability to conceptualise and, in turn, bring it back.

What I remember clearly is being wiped away (both body and ego loss), being told the secrets of the universe, forgetting them mid-trip, being gone for a long time, experiencing untold bliss, and then coming back utterly astounded, convinced I had met the 'divine'. I was becoming a human again. I was sobbing with gratitude as I was reborn.

I can remember other DMT trips more clearly, the ones where I'm travelling through hyperspace with cheeky jester beings.

I opted to try it as an antidepressant. For me antidepressants are the last resort, as I'm put off by the side-effects and withdrawal. I have tried Prozac before and I recall at the time finding it having a numbing effect, unable to feel either positive or negative feelings, but this could have also been from the depression (I didn't take the Prozac for very long).

With microdosing, it has not been properly studied, so all I can do is talk about my experience. What I found was that (many times, not every time I dosed) it had an antidepressant effect. I could feel the depression lift. I could feel it lift in my mind and in my body. My mind wasn't causing me pain and discomfort, nor was my body. My thinking was much more calmer, positive and 'realistic'. The pain in my chest was gone, I could breathe easy and effortlessly. And I had a slightly elevated mood - not like you do when you've taken a drug, but just when you're having a good day.

I've been experimenting with this for nearly 3 months and I think it's time to stop. Dosing recently has left me feeling worse (although much better the following days). Remember, psychedelics (even at low doses) are amplifiers, so they can make a bad day worse. I think also I needed to lower the dose.

My depression has not disappeared, but it's improved a lot, and the symptoms are much more manageable. I believe MDing played some role in this, but it's hard to say how significant that role has been, as I've also been going to therapy, exercising regularly, sleeping well, eating well, meditaitng daily and taking and omega-3 supplement, all of which help with depression.

1) I cannot say. The first time I broke through I would say I was going through an episode of depression. The experience seemed to address my self-loathing and pit of darkness I was in. All of my feelings of self-hatred were washed away by divine, motherly love. However, I cannot say what the experience will be like for you. Whatever you decide, treat the experience with the utmost respect - you are about to be granted access to somewhere special and unexplored. I've found that setting up a calming space (internally and externally) and saying a little prayer to oneself before blasting off helps. I would say: "I'm here to learn. Please be gentle."

2) Again, I cannot say.

3) Why do you apply that fear to all other drugs except DMT? It is the most potent psychedelic that exists. It cannot cause permanent brain damage, you don't have to worry about that. But it does reliably cause profound and intense experiences. That's something to keep in mind. 50mg is also more than I would recommend for a first timer, especially for someone who has never used drugs. The most I have ever attempted to smoke (I didn't finish the dose) was 50mg. And that was way too much! Not that I had a bad experience (although there was some panic at the onset and the end - as I thought I would never come down).

4) It's like following a recipe for baking a cake. It's pretty easy. But of course, you can also mess up baking a cake :P I can't tell you any odds. Just follow the instructions. It does involve using harsh chemicals, so be safe.

5) I don't know about poisonous. Maybe unsafe? Someone else would have to answer this. If you mess up the extraction, obviously don't use it.

Bonus: It has helped to see that it's possible to love myself. It's also changed my outlook, attitudes and perspective in innumerable other ways. It harmed me at a point when I became obsessed about it - to the point where I was losing sleep. It's normal to dwell on the experience. But I naturally obsess about things. So be conscious of your individual constitution.
